simple: This page introduces the older way to add sound in Roblox, using the `Sound` object. Roblox now has a newer set of audio objects that can do more, but `Sound` still shows up in lots of games and tutorials, so it helps to know it. Where you put a `Sound` in the Explorer decides whether players hear it everywhere or only near a spot. You can also group sounds together and add effects like echo or muffling.
analogy: A `Sound` inside a part is like a radio sitting on a table: you hear it louder as you walk up to it. A `Sound` in SoundService is like music in your headphones: the same wherever you go.
keyPoints: This is the legacy (older) sound system; the newer audio objects are recommended for new work.
Each audio file has an ID you put into a `Sound` object's `SoundId` to choose what it plays.
A sound can play automatically when the game starts, or a script can start it.
Put a `Sound` inside a part or `Attachment` to make it positional, so players only hear it nearby.
Put a `Sound` directly in Workspace or SoundService to make it background audio heard everywhere.
A `SoundGroup` works like a mixer that controls the volume and effects of many sounds at once.
Dynamic effects like `EqualizerSoundEffect`, `CompressorSoundEffect`, and `ReverbSoundEffect` change how a sound or group sounds.

terms.legacy: An older feature that still works but has a newer replacement.
terms.audio asset: A sound file uploaded to Roblox, with its own ID number.
terms.runtime: When the game is actually running and being played.
terms.positional audio: Sound that comes from a spot in the world and gets quieter as you move away from it.
terms.background audio: Sound that is the same volume no matter where you stand, like a soundtrack.
terms.parent: The object something sits inside in the Explorer. If a `Sound` is inside a part, the part is its parent.
terms.audio mixer: A tool that lets you adjust the volume of many sounds together, like sliders on a DJ board.
terms.dynamic effect: An object that changes how a sound comes out, like adding echo or muffling it.

watchOut: If you want everyone to hear music everywhere, do not put the `Sound` inside a part. Put it in SoundService or Workspace.
If a sound seems to play from nowhere, check its parent; a `Sound` in Workspace plays for the whole game.
For brand-new projects, try the newer audio objects first, since `Sound` is the older system.
